subject: Career
title: Nonverbal Communication: The Silent 93%
description: A quick win: understand Nonverbal Communication: The Silent 93%.

hook.text: Albert Mehrabian's research: 55% of communication is body language, 38% tone, and only 7% words.

buildup.text: When your words say 'I'm fine' but your body says otherwise, people believe the body.

discovery.text: Eye contact, posture, gestures, and facial expressions transmit trust, confidence, and engagement.

twist.text: Mehrabian's numbers apply to emotional messages specifically. But the principle holds: nonverbal signals dominate.

climax.text: In video calls, these signals are reduced. Exaggerate slightly: nod more, lean in, use facial reactions.

punchline.text: People hear your words. They believe your body.

quiz.question: What percentage of emotional communication is body language according to Mehrabian?

details.summary: Albert Mehrabian's research is often cited as showing that 93 percent of communication is nonverbal, though this applies specifically to situations involving emotional ambiguity. In the workplace, body language, facial expressions, and vocal tone do heavily influence how messages are received.
details.whyItMatters: Leaders whose verbal and nonverbal signals conflict create confusion and distrust. Aligning body language with spoken words strengthens credibility and message impact.
takeaways: Nonverbal cues dominate when verbal messages are ambiguous
Gestures and posture signal confidence or uncertainty instantly
Practicing open body language improves perceived leadership

faq.question: Is the 93 percent nonverbal statistic actually accurate?
faq.answer: Mehrabian's original study focused specifically on the communication of feelings and attitudes, not all communication. In those emotional contexts, nonverbal cues dominate. For factual information, words carry more weight. The principle remains directionally useful.

faq.question: How can I improve my nonverbal communication at work?
faq.answer: Record yourself during a practice presentation. Watch for crossed arms, lack of eye contact, and fidgeting. Practice maintaining open posture, steady eye contact, and purposeful gestures. Small adjustments in posture significantly change how others perceive your confidence.
